=== Morphological Assessment Form ===
A. Leaf Arrangement & Architecture
    1. Leaf relative position (alternate / opposite / whorled): alternate (leaves are attached at successive nodes along the stem, alternating sides; no paired leaves or whorls visible)
    2. Leaf spacing (clustered / distal): clustered (multiple leaves are grouped closely along the upper portion of the stem, especially near the apex)

B. Leaf Complexity
    3. Leaf complexity (simple / compound): simple (each leaf blade is undivided and attached directly to the petiole)
    4. Compound leaf type, ONLY if leaf complexity is compound (odd-pinnate / even-pinnate): N/A
    5. Number of leaflets (integer estimate 2, 4, 8, …): N/A
    6. Leaflet arrangement (opposite / alternate / subopposite): N/A

C. Leaf Morphology
    7. Leaf margin (entire / toothed) AND if toothed (dentate, serrate, etc.)): entire (margins are smooth and unbroken; no teeth or serrations observed)
    8. Leaf shape (elliptic, obovate, lanceolate, etc.): elliptic (leaves are broadest near the middle and taper to both ends, with a symmetrical outline)
    9. Leaf apex (acute, obtuse, acuminate): acute (tip is pointed but not sharply drawn out)
    10. Leaf base (rounded, cordate, cuneate): rounded (base is gently curved and not tapering or heart-shaped)
    11. Venation type (pinnate / palmate / parallel): pinnate (main vein runs from base to apex, with secondary veins branching off and curving toward the margin)
    12. Secondary veins (visibility, spacing, number): visible, closely spaced, multiple pairs (secondary veins are clearly visible, forming a network, with 4-6 pairs per leaf, running parallel to each other and curving toward the margin)
    13. Leaf surface features (glabrous, shiny, dull, rugose): shiny, rugose (surface has a glossy appearance and is slightly wrinkled or textured, especially along veins)
    14. Leaf surface trichomes (present / absent): absent (no visible hairs or projections on leaf surface)
    15. Petiole length (short / long): short (petioles are relatively short, less than half the length of the leaf blade)
    16. Petiole features (winged / grooved / terete): terete (petioles are round in cross-section, without wings or grooves)

D. Stem & Shoot Traits
    17. Stem type, may not be visible (woody / herbaceous): woody (stems are firm, dark green to brownish, and appear lignified, consistent with woody growth)

    20. Stem texture (smooth / ridged / lenticellate): smooth (stems appear smooth without ridges or visible lenticels)

E. Other Visible Seedling Traits
    21. Stipules, sometimes visible only in close-up images (present / absent): absent (no stipules observed at leaf bases; nodes appear clean)
    22. Latex, rarely visible but extremely diagnostic when present (present / not observed): not observed (no exudate visible when stems or leaves are damaged)
    23. Pulvinus, for Fabaceae family only (present / absent): absent (no swollen joint at leaf base; not applicable to this morphology)

Locating an individual
It is mainly observed towards the Southern Boundary (LS), Quebrada El Salto, etc., in rolling or broken terrain.
Distribution
From Belize to Venezuela, the Guianas, Brazil, and Bolivia. In Costa Rica, it is widely distributed in the medium to low elevations of both slopes, in climates ranging from humid to very humid, although it prefers climates with marked seasonality; 0-700-800 m.
Habit
Trees, 15-35 m tall.
Trunk
Trunk with reddish-brown outer bark.
Bark
Outer bark reddish-brown, scaly, inner bark reddish with a pleasant mango scent; white or milky resinous sap.
Leaves
Odd-pinnate leaves, with 7-9 leaflets, elliptical, oblong, or oblong-lanceolate, 5-21 x 4-7.2 cm, apex acuminate to abruptly acuminate, base obtuse to asymmetric, generally glabrous; petiolules without evident pulvini, margin entire; petioles 4-14 cm long.
Flowers
Inflorescences are panicles, 3-15 cm long, axillary. Yellowish or greenish-yellow flowers (unisexual); calyx with 5 lobes, 1-1.5 mm long, cuculiform; petals (tubular corolla), with 5 lobes, 5-5.5 mm long; stamens 10, 1 mm long, filaments inserted at the base of the disc; annular disc with 10 lobes; ovary with 5 lobes, ovoid, with 5 locules; style 1, stigma with 5 lobes.
Fruits
Capsular and drupe-like fruits, 1.5-2.5 x 1.5 x 3 cm, ovoid or more or less turbinate, with 2-5 lobes, dehiscent by 4-5 valves, scarlet red inside, red to black when mature; pyrenes 3-5, 12-13 mm thick, white, the mesocarp (pseudoaril) reddish turning white upon exposure (dehiscence), fleshy, juicy, sweet, and edible.
Diagnosis
Characterized by being a large tree, the bark on mature trees is somewhat scaly, lenticellate, and the inner bark has a very particular and pleasant mango scent. At the vegetative level, it is sometimes confused with the genus Protium, although its leaves lack pulvinated petiolules and the turpentine aroma when crushed. Its fruits are distinctive for their peculiar turbinate shape.
Habitat
In the Forest; it is mainly observed towards the Southern Boundary (LS), Quebrada El Salto, etc., in rolling or broken terrain.
Phenology
Flowers observed in June and August; fruits in August and February.

Shrub or tree, 1-10(-18) m, the twigs brown; stipules deciduous (but sometimes present with submature leaves). Leaves opposite or with a cuspidate apex, often puberulent and (often) entire or serrated (with the glands of the teeth). Petiole 0.2-0.4 cm, lamina 3.5-11 cm, also hirsute on the midrib on the underside. Flowers with the pedicel articulated at the base; sepals 1/4-1/3 the length of the petals, acute to rounded at the apex, indistinctly 1-3-nerved; petals whitish to pale yellow or orange, 3.5-4.2 mm, glabrous or glabrate; stamens with the connective scale extended laterally and apically (< the total length of the anther), subentire; style 1.252 mm. Fruits 1.5-1.9 cm, slightly velvety; seeds 4-8 mm, glabrous. Wet and very wet forest, 0-600+ m; Caribbean slope and near the Continental Divide, Cordilleras of Guanacaste and Talamanca, Plains of Los Guatusos, Tortuguero, and Santa Clara, Lower Talamanca, Pacific slope N Cord. of Talamanca (Cerro Nara), S Nicoya Peninsula, P.N. Carara, Puriscal region (P.N. La Cangreja), vicinity of Palmar Norte, Gulf Dulce region, Burica Peninsula. Fl. Jan., Mar.—May, Jul., Nov. SE Hond.—Pan. [The fruits with the pedicel articulated at the base and glabrous seeds] easily distinguish Rinorea squamata from its congeners in Costa Rica with opposite leaves. Due to its densely puberulent leaf blades and (often) also hirsute on the midrib on the underside, Rinorea squamata is somewhat similar to Rinorea sylvatica, but vegetatively very different due to its smaller stipules and blades with the glands of the acicular teeth (vs. broadly conical).

Trees, climbing shrubs, or lianas; stipules absent. Leaves compound, odd-pinnate or trifoliate, indumentum of simple trichomes, the blade sometimes with glandular dots on the underside, margin entire; petiole and petiolules pulvinated. Inflorescences in panicles, racemes, or spike-like, axillary or terminal. Flowers bisexual, white, yellowish, or pale pink; sepals 5, valvate or imbricate; petals 5, free; stamens 10, forming a short tube at the base; ovary superior, carpels 1-5, style one per carpel; ovules 2 per carpel. Fruit in follicles, often red; seeds 1 per fruit, black, the aril bright red, yellow, white, or orange.
The family consists of 16 genera and about 300–350 species, pantropical, with a distribution center in western Africa; for tropical America, 5 genera and 108 species are known; 3 genera and 9 species in CR.
It is characterized by its compound leaves, mainly trifoliate or odd-pinnate, leaflets alternate on the rachis, sometimes with dendritic trichomes, petioles clearly pulvinated, stipules absent, and the fruit follicles with a black seed with a reddish basal aril. In vegetative form, its general appearance relates it directly to the family Fabaceae, but several of the characteristics mentioned earlier allow it to be separated.
Traditionally, the family has been placed within the Order Rosales, or in close relation to the Order Sapindales, and some have suggested a link between such Orders. However, recent molecular studies suggest that its placement is in the Order Oxalidales, along with families such as: Oxalidaceae, Cunnoniaceae, Elaeocarpaceae, etc.

Shrub or tree, (2-)8-20 m, the crown dense and rounded; young branches cylindrical. Leaves with brown petiole, 0.7-2 cm; blade 4.3-19.3 X 2.5-10.2 cm, elliptical to ovate-oblong, attenuate to obtuse and often oblique at the base, abruptly acuminate at the apex, subcoriaceous or thinly coriaceous, flexible, thin and ± densely tuberculate (but shiny) on the adaxial surface (in dry specimens). Inflorescences with 6-10 flowers. Flowers white or greenish, aromatic; calyx crateriform, 5-lobed, in fruit spreading, pink to red, 15-26 mm in diameter, lobed. Fruits white or yellowish-green when ripe, 1-1.5 X 0.8-1 cm, broadly ellipsoid to subglobose, vermicular. Very wet forest, 0-300(-600) m; Caribbean slope, Central Cordillera (E.B. Fa Selva) and Talamanca, basin of the Sapoá River, Tortuguero lowland, Pacific slope, Montes del Aguacate, P.N. Carara, P. N. Manuel Antonio, Osa Peninsula. Flowering Jan., Feb., Apr.-Jun., Aug., Nov., Dec. Recognized by its often tree-like habit, leaf blades thin and densely tuberculate (but shiny) on the adaxial surface and fruits white or yellowish-green.

Tree, ca. 5-30(-40) m. Leaves imparipinnate, 10-30 cm; petiole and rachis generally canaliculate, glabrous or sparsely puberulent; leaflets 5-9, alternate (rarely subopposite), 10-15(-20) X 2.5-4.5 cm, narrowly elliptical or oblong to oblanceolate, attenuated at the base, acute to acuminate at the apex, subcoriaceous, generally glabrous, with 13-16 secondary veins per side. Inflorescences axillary, thyrsoid, 10-20 cm, glabrous or puberulent. Flowers with petals white to yellowish-green. Fruits yellow to orange, 1.4-2 X 0.8-1.2 cm, oblong to ellipsoid, densely verrucous (with prominent warts often connected by irregular stripes), often sparsely adpressed-pubescent, with 3 or 4 valves; seeds 1 or 2, black, 0.8-2.2 cm, the aril red. Very humid forest, 0-350 m; Pacific slope, [in the Parque Nacional Carara], [in the Puriscal region (in the Parque Nacional La Cangreja)], [in the Parque Nacional Manuel Antonio], [in Uvita], [in the Gulf Dulce region]. Fl. Feb.-Apr., Jun., Dec. [in Costa Rica and Panama], [in Ecuador and Peru], [in Northeast Brazil].

Shrub, 1-1.8 m tall; stems and leaves glabrate. Stipules persistent, 3-5 mm long, bifid to near base, the lobes distant, acuminate; petioles 1-1.5 cm long; blades ± elliptic, acute to acuminate, cuneate at base, 10-16 (20) cm long, 4-6 cm wide, drying light green. Racemes short, terminal, usually to 1.5 cm long at anthesis, to 3 cm long in fruit; peduncles lacking or to 1.2 cm long; inflorescence branches, pedicels, and calyces with short, ± erect, sparse trichomes, the lowermost branches subtended by a distinct, oblong-elliptic bract ca 5 mm long; bracts green, ovate, 2-7 mm long, acute, foliate, persistent, subtending groups of 2-4(7) flowers, exceeding the flowers; flowers white, sessile, ca 3.5 mm long, the tube ca 2 mm long, the lobes oblong, to ca 1.5 mm long; filaments ca 0.5 mm long, affixed above the middle of the tube; anthers ca 1 mm long; style ca 4 mm long; stigmas 0.2 mm long. Berries ± globose, 3-4 mm diam, flattened laterally and somewhat grooved, glabrous or sparsely puberulent at least when immature; seeds 2, flat, with a deep groove on the inside surface, rounded and 4- or 5-grooved on the outside surface. Croat 11132. Apparently rare; found in the younger forest south of Fairchild Point and in the forest north of Barbour Trail. Flowers mostly from June to September, principally in July, rarely also in the dry season. The fruits mature from July to October, principally in August. In Panama, Psychotria brachybotrya is most easily confused with Psychotria involucrata Sw., a superfluous name for Psychotria officinalis (Aubl.) Sw. (Steyermark, 1972). Psychotria brachybotrya differs from Psychotria officinalis by having distinct bracts beneath the lower inflorescence branches and leaves that usually dry a lighter green. Psychotria brachybotrya usually occurs in drier areas than Psychotria officinalis, which occurs principally in premontane wet forest and tropical wet forest. Psychotria brachybotrya has also been confused with Psychotria furcata DC, but is distinguished from Psychotria furcata by its larger, lighter-colored leaves and green, rather than purple, inflorescence bracts. Psychotria brachybotrya is distributed from Panama to Colombia, Venezuela, the Guianas, Brazil, Peru, and Bolivia; Trinidad. Dioecious, hemiepiphytic tree, to 10 m tall; trunk to 15 cm dbh; branches spiraled, stiff and spreading, densely rooting at the nodes, the roots often extending back to the host tree and enveloping the host tree for support; stems glabrous with prominent leaf scars; sap pale yellow to bright orange (in time), not copious. Panicles stout, bracteated, divaricately branched, terminal; buds depressed-globose; pedicels stout, to 1 cm long; flowers thick, 5-parted, spreading at anthesis, to 4.5 cm diam, white to pink, the lobes often marked with maroon or magenta at base or apex; sepals 2, concave, unequal, persisting in fruit; petals 4-10, broadly oblong, 2-2.5 cm long; androecium of staminate flowers cushion-shaped, ca 1 cm wide and 5 mm high with numerous anthers; pollen white, granular, compressed in round or oval pouches ca 1 mm diam, embedded just beneath the sticky surface of the disk; pistillate flowers similar to staminate but the gynoecium divided into (4)9(15) segments, the petals falling soon after anthesis, the sepals closing. Capsules subglobose, 2.5-3 cm long, dehiscing into 5-9 parts at maturity; valves thick, ± spreading to expose the colorful mass of seeds; seeds numerous, reddish, curved-oblong, ca 5 mm long, embedded in a deeply divided, bright-orange aril. Frequent epiphyte in the forest or on exposed shorelines; epiphytic on rocks or on trees near the edge of the water. Plants are usually supported on tree trunks or large branches but the branches may grow into the top of the canopy. Apparently flowers and fruits sporadically throughout the year. Where plants occur along the shore, the branches usually root at the nodes with the roots hanging in the water. The pollen sacs of the staminate flowers burst under the slightest pressure, and abundant pollen oozes out (sometimes explosively).
